Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}\in H$ write $v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1}\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor.

(a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with

$$U_\pi(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=v_{\pi^{-1}(0)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n-1)},$$

and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$.

(b) The operators

$$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$

(with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections.

(c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$.

(d) If $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}$ have a repeated factor, that is, $v_i=v_j$ for some distinct $i,j\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, then $P_-(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=0$.

Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). By the orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]) every $x\in H$ has a unique representation

$$x=P_Mx+(x-P_Mx),\qquad P_Mx\in M,\quad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp ,$$

and the **Hilbert orthogonal projection onto $M$** is the map

$$P_M:H\longrightarrow M\subseteq H,\qquad x\longmapsto P_Mx ,$$

assigning to $x$ its unique $M$-component. Its defining properties are therefore

$$P_Mx\in M,\qquad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp\qquad(x\in H),$$

which characterise $P_M$ uniquely: a map with these defining properties must agree with the $M$-component of the unique decomposition of each $x$.

**Agreement with the finite-dimensional projection.** If $V$ is a finite-dimensional inner-product space and $W\subseteq V$ a subspace, then [[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]] writes $V=W\oplus W^\perp$ and [[def-orthogonal-projection]] defines $P_Wv$ as the unique $W$-component of $v$; the defining properties displayed above are the same, so they define the same map on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.

**Range and kernel.** $P_Mx\in M$ for every $x$, and $P_Mm=m$ for $m\in M$ because $m=m+0$ with $0\in M^\perp$; conversely $P_Mx=0$ says exactly that $x=x-0\in M^\perp$. Hence the range of $P_M$ is $M$ and its kernel is $M^\perp$, and $P_M$ is the identity on $M$ and zero on $M^\perp$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

For a finite set $A$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$ put

$$[A]^{k} := \{\, S \subseteq A \ :\ \lvert S\rvert = k \,\},$$

the set of $k$-element subsets of $A$. Every $S \subseteq A$ is finite
([[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]]), so the condition $\lvert S\rvert = k$ makes
sense for every subset.

**$[A]^{k}$ is finite.** It is a subset of $\mathcal{P}(A)$, which is finite by
[[cor-cardinality-of-the-power-set]], so [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]] applies.

**$\lvert [A]^{k}\rvert$ depends only on $\lvert A\rvert$.** Let $h : A \to A'$ be
a bijection of finite sets. The direct image map $S \mapsto h[S]$ carries
$[A]^{k}$ into $[A']^{k}$, because $h$ restricted to $S$ is a bijection of $S$
onto $h[S]$ and so $\lvert h[S]\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = k$ by the transport
clause of [[def-finite-cardinality]]; the map $T \mapsto h^{-1}[T]$ is its
two-sided inverse, since $h^{-1}[h[S]] = S$ and $h[h^{-1}[T]] = T$ for a
bijection $h$. So $[A]^{k} \approx [A']^{k}$ and the two have the same
cardinality.

**Definition.** For $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$ set

$$\binom{n}{k} := \big\lvert\, [n]^{k} \,\big\rvert \in \mathbb{N},$$

the **binomial coefficient**. By the previous paragraph and $\lvert n\rvert = n$,

$$\big\lvert [A]^{k}\big\rvert = \binom{\lvert A\rvert}{k} \qquad \text{for every finite } A .$$

**$\binom{n}{k}$ is a count, so it is a natural number by construction.** It is
*not* defined as $n!/(k!\,(n-k)!)$: that expression involves a division, hence
lives in $\mathbb{R}$, and the assertion that its value is a natural number is a
theorem, proved in [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]]. Defining the coefficient as a
count makes integrality free and leaves the closed formula something to prove.

**Boundary values, read off the definition and not stipulated.**

- $\binom{n}{0} = 1$ **for every $n$, including $n = 0$**: the subsets of $n$ of
  cardinality $0$ are exactly the subsets equal to $\varnothing$
  ([[def-finite-cardinality]], clause (b)), so $[n]^{0} = \{\varnothing\}$, a
  one-element set. No empty-product convention is involved.
- $\binom{n}{n} = 1$: if $S \subseteq n$ has $\lvert S\rvert = n = \lvert n\rvert$
  then $S = n$ by clause 3 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $[n]^{n} = \{n\}$.
- $\binom{n}{k} = 0$ for $k > n$: a subset $S \subseteq n$ has
  $\lvert S\rvert \le n$ by clause 2 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $\lvert S\rvert = k > n$ is impossible and $[n]^{k} = \varnothing$
  ([[lem-nat-trichotomy]]).
- $\binom{n}{1} = n$: a subset of cardinality $1$ is $\{x\}$ for exactly one
  $x \in n$, since $\lvert S\rvert = 1$ means $S \approx \{0\}$; so
  $S \mapsto$ its unique element is a bijection $[n]^{1} \to n$.
- $\binom{0}{0} = 1$ and $\binom{0}{k} = 0$ for $k \ge 1$, both instances of the
  above.

Let $m \ge 1$ and write $m = \sigma(M)$, so $M = m-1$. Then for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$

$$\big\lvert\mathcal{W}(n,m)\big\rvert = \binom{n+m-1}{\,m-1\,} = \binom{n+M}{M},$$

and the map
$k \mapsto \big\{\, \big(\sum_{j<\sigma(i)} k_j\big) + i \ :\ i < M \,\big\}$
is a bijection of $\mathcal{W}(n,m)$ onto the set of $M$-element subsets of
$n+M$.

Moreover, for $m \ge 1$ **and $n \ge 1$**,

$$\big\lvert\mathcal{C}(n,m)\big\rvert = \binom{n-1}{\,m-1\,}.$$

**The hypothesis $m \ge 1$ is not decoration.** At $m = 0$ the expression
$\binom{n+m-1}{m-1}$ would require the value $m-1$ at $m = 0$, and
[[def-composition-of-a-natural-number]] records the true counts there:
$\lvert\mathcal{W}(0,0)\rvert = 1$ and $\lvert\mathcal{W}(n,0)\rvert = 0$ for
$n \ge 1$. The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ in the second display is equally load
bearing: at $n = 0$, $m = 1$ the formula would give $\binom{0}{0} = 1$ while
$\mathcal{C}(0,1) = \varnothing$.

Let $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$ with $k \le n$. Then, in $\mathbb{N}$,

$$\binom{n}{k}\cdot k!\cdot (n-k)! = n! ,$$

and consequently:

1. $\binom{n}{k}\cdot k! = n^{\underline{k}}$
   ([[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]);
2. **integrality**: in $\mathbb{R}$,
   $\iota\binom{n}{k} = \dfrac{\iota(n!)}{\iota(k!)\,\iota((n-k)!)}$, so the
   familiar quotient $n!/(k!\,(n-k)!)$ is the canonical natural of a natural
   number, namely of the count $\binom{n}{k}$;
3. **symmetry**: $\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n}{n-k}$.

Here $\iota$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]] and $n-k$ the
truncated difference, which for $k \le n$ is the ordinary one.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
for $x\in H$ and finite $F\subseteq I$ put

$$P_Fx:=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i .$$

Then the following four assertions are equivalent:

1. **(completeness)** the closed linear span of $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ is $H$;
2. **(zero complement)** the only vector orthogonal to every $e_i$ is $0$;
3. **(Parseval)** $\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2=\|x\|^2$
   for every $x\in H$, the sum being the supremum of the finite subsums
   ([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]);
4. **(net convergence)** the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$
   converges to $x$ for every $x\in H$.

Assertion 2 is the statement
$\operatorname{span}\{e_i : i\in I\}^\perp=\{0\}$
([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

derivations.claim: [Product basis] We show by induction on $n\ge1$ that $(e_i)_{i\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n}$ is an orthonormal basis of $H^{\otimes n}$. For $n=1$ this is the hypothesis. If it holds for $n$, then by [F1] applied to the orthonormal basis $(e_i)_{i\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n}$ of $H^{\otimes n}$ and $(e_j)_{j\in\{1,\dots,d\}}$ of $H$, the products $e_i\otimes e_j$ form an orthonormal family with dense span in $H^{\otimes(n+1)}=H^{\otimes n}\widehat\otimes H$. This family is finite, indexed by $Q:=\{1,\dots,d\}^n\times\{1,\dots,d\}$. Its span is closed: if $z_r=\sum_{q\in Q}c_{r,q}g_q\to z$, where $g_q$ denotes the corresponding product vector, orthonormality gives $\|z_r-z_s\|^2=\sum_{q\in Q}|c_{r,q}-c_{s,q}|^2$, so each coefficient sequence is Cauchy. Let $c_q$ be its limit in $\mathbb C$; the same finite norm identity gives $z_r\to\sum_{q\in Q}c_qg_q$, hence $z=\sum_{q\in Q}c_qg_q$ lies in the span. Since the span is also dense, it equals the whole tensor product. Thus the family is an orthonormal basis, its cardinality is $d\cdot d^n=d^{n+1}$ and $\dim H^{\otimes(n+1)}=d^{n+1}$. This proves the induction step and (a).

[The alternating projection on basis vectors] Let $i\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n$. By the action formula of [F2], $P_-^{(n)}(e_i)=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)e_{i_{\widehat{\pi}^{-1}(1)}}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_{\widehat{\pi}^{-1}(n)}}=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\tau\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\tau)e_{i_{\widehat{\tau}(1)}}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_{\widehat{\tau}(n)}}$ after the substitution $\tau=\pi^{-1}$. If two entries of $i$ coincide, say $i_k=i_l$ with $k\ne l$, then the transposition $\upsilon=(k-1\;l-1)$ satisfies $e_{i_{\widehat{\upsilon\tau}(1)}}\otimes\cdots=e_{i_{\widehat{\tau}(1)}}\otimes\cdots$ for every $\tau$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(\upsilon\tau)=-\operatorname{sgn}(\tau)$, so the sum pairs to zero and $P_-^{(n)}(e_i)=0$ by [F2]. If the entries are pairwise distinct with underlying set $J=\{j_1<\cdots<j_n\}$ and $i_k=j_{\widehat{\rho_i}(k)}$, then $e_{i_{\widehat{\tau}(1)}}\otimes\cdots=e_{j_{\widehat{\rho_i\tau}(1)}}\otimes\cdots$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(\tau)=\operatorname{sgn}(\rho_i)\operatorname{sgn}(\rho_i\tau)$; substituting $\omega=\rho_i\tau$ gives $P_-^{(n)}(e_i)=\frac{\operatorname{sgn}(\rho_i)}{n!}\sum_{\omega\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\omega)e_{j_{\widehat{\omega}(1)}}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_{\widehat{\omega}(n)}}=\operatorname{sgn}(\rho_i)\frac{e_J^\wedge}{\sqrt{n!}}$, which is the second formula of (b).

[Orthonormality of the Slater family] For subsets $J,K$ with $|J|=|K|=n$ let $A$ be the canonical matrix with $A(a-1,b-1)=\langle e_{j_a},e_{k_b}\rangle=\delta_{j_a,k_b}$, and abbreviate this entry as $A_{ab}$ for $1\le a,b\le n$. By [F1], $\langle e_J^\wedge,e_K^\wedge\rangle=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma,\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{l=1}^n A_{\widehat{\sigma}(l),\widehat{\pi}(l)}$. For each fixed $\pi$ substitute $\sigma=\omega\pi$ and reindex the product by $t=\widehat{\pi}(l)$. Then $\prod_l A_{\widehat{\sigma}(l),\widehat{\pi}(l)}=\prod_t A_{\widehat{\omega}(t),t}$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)=\operatorname{sgn}(\omega)$, so the sum over $\pi$ contributes $n!$ and the remaining sum is $\det(A)$ by [F3]. For $J=K$, $A=I_n$ and this is $1$; for $J\ne K$, some $j_a$ is absent from $K$, giving a zero row and determinant $0$. Thus the Slater family is orthonormal.

[Occupation operators] For $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ the formula of (d) defines a linear endomorphism of the finite-dimensional space $H^{\otimes n}$; by [F6] applied to the complete orthonormal family $(e_i)$ we have $x=\sum_i\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$ and $N_jx=\sum_i|i|_j\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$ for every $x$. Self-adjointness: for $x,y\in H^{\otimes n}$ the expansions give $\langle N_jx,y\rangle=\sum_i|i|_j\langle x,e_i\rangle\overline{\langle y,e_i\rangle}=\langle x,N_jy\rangle$ because the numbers $|i|_j$ are real, so $N_j$ is self-adjoint by [F7]; it is bounded because its range is spanned by the finitely many $e_i$ with eigenvalue at most $n$, and $\|N_jx\|\le n\|x\|$. The same computation on the basis vectors $e_i$, on which $N_j$ is diagonal with the real eigenvalues $|i|_j$, gives $N_jN_ke_i=|i|_k|i|_je_i=N_kN_je_i$ and $\sum_jN_je_i=\bigl(\sum_j|i|_j\bigr)e_i=ne_i$; since the $e_i$ form a basis by step 1.1 and both sides of each identity are linear, $N_jN_k=N_kN_j$ and $\sum_{j=1}^dN_j=nI$. This proves the operator statements of (d) except the two eigenvector formulas.

[Slater basis and its dimension] By step 1.2 each $e_J^\wedge=\sqrt{n!}\,P_-^{(n)}(e_{j_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_n})$ lies in $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}$, and each $P_-^{(n)}(e_i)$ is either zero or a multiple of some $e_J^\wedge$; since the $e_i$ form a basis of $H^{\otimes n}$ by step 1.1 and $P_-^{(n)}$ is linear, the closed linear span of $(e_J^\wedge)$ is exactly $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}$ (a finite-dimensional, hence closed, subspace). By step 1.3 the family is orthonormal, so it is an orthonormal basis of $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}$, indexed by the $n$-element subsets $J$ of $\{1,\dots,d\}$; by [F4] there are $\binom dn$ of them, so $\dim\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}=\binom dn$. If $n>d$, then two of the $n$ entries of any $i$ coincide, so $P_-^{(n)}(e_i)=0$ for every basis vector $e_i$ by step 1.2, whence $P_-^{(n)}=0$ and $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}=\{0\}$. In particular $e_J^\wedge\ne0$ whenever $|J|=n\le d$. This completes (b).

[The symmetric sums] Fix $\lambda\in W(n,d)$. The word $c$ that lists $1$ with multiplicity $\lambda_1$, then $2$ with multiplicity $\lambda_2$, and so on through $d$ has $|c|=\lambda$, so $\operatorname{orb}(\lambda)
e\varnothing$ and $m_\lambda=\sum_{c\in\operatorname{orb}(\lambda)}e_c$ is a nonempty sum of orthonormal vectors of $H^{\otimes n}$, hence nonzero, with $\|m_\lambda\|^2=|\operatorname{orb}(\lambda)|$ by the orthonormality of the product basis in step 1.1 [F1]. If $\lambda
e\mu$ then a word has a unique multiplicity vector, so $\operatorname{orb}(\lambda)\cap\operatorname{orb}(\mu)=\varnothing$ and the inner product of $m_\lambda$ and $m_\mu$ is the empty sum $0$. For $\pi\in S_n$ the map $c\mapsto\pi\cdot c$, $(\pi\cdot c)_k:=c_{\widehat{\pi}^{-1}(k)}$, permutes $\operatorname{orb}(\lambda)$ and $U_\pi e_c=e_{\pi\cdot c}$ by [F2], so $U_\pi m_\lambda=m_\lambda$. Finally, $P_+^{(n)}e_i= rac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}e_{\pi\cdot i}$ has coefficients supported on $\operatorname{orb}(|i|)$; for $c\in\operatorname{orb}(|i|)$ the set $\{\pi:\pi\cdot i=c\}$ is the coset $\pi_0\operatorname{Stab}(i)$ for any $\pi_0$ with $\pi_0\cdot i=c$, hence has cardinality $|\operatorname{Stab}(i)|\ge1$, and it is empty for $c
otin\operatorname{orb}(|i|)$; therefore $P_+^{(n)}e_i=\gamma_i\,m_{|i|}$ with $\gamma_i:=|\operatorname{Stab}(i)|/n!>0$. This proves all the assertions of (c) except the dimension.

[Symmetric basis and its dimension] By step 2.3 the $m_\lambda$ are nonzero, pairwise orthogonal and lie in $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ (indeed $m_\lambda=\gamma_i^{-1}P_+^{(n)}e_i$ for any multi-index $i$ with $|i|=\lambda$, and such $i$ exists because $\lambda\in W(n,d)$); conversely every $P_+^{(n)}e_i$ is a multiple of some $m_\lambda$, so by linearity and the basis property of the $e_i$ the span of $(m_\lambda)_{\lambda\in W(n,d)}$ is $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$. A pairwise orthogonal family of nonzero vectors spanning a finite-dimensional space is a basis, so $\dim\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}=|W(n,d)|=\binom{n+d-1}{d-1}=\binom{n+d-1}{n}$ by [F5]. This completes (c).

[Occupation numbers on the two bases] Every summand $e_c$ of $e_J^\wedge$ has exactly one entry equal to $j$ when $j\in J$ and none otherwise, so $|c|_j=\mathbf 1_J(j)$ for every such $c$; and every $c\in\operatorname{orb}(\lambda)$ has $|c|_j=\lambda_j$. Since the $N_j$ are linear and act diagonally on the $e_c$ by the formula of step 2.1, this gives $N_je_J^\wedge=\mathbf 1_J(j)e_J^\wedge$ and $N_jm_\lambda=\lambda_jm_\lambda$, the remaining assertions of (d). Both basis families displayed in (b) and (c) therefore consist of joint eigenvectors of $(N_1,\dots,N_d)$, and the two maps $J\mapsto\mathbf 1_J$ and $\lambda\mapsto\lambda$ are injective; hence the joint eigenspaces inside the two sectors are the lines spanned by the corresponding basis vectors, as asserted in (d), and each sector is invariant under every $N_j$.

[Assembly] Step 1.1 proves (a), steps 1.2, 1.3 and 2.2 prove (b), steps 2.3 and 3.1 prove (c), and steps 2.1 and 4.1 prove (d). The proof uses only the completed tensor powers, the permutation projections, the orthonormal expansions and the stated counting facts, under the Countable Choice hypothesis of [F1] and [F2]; no physical reading of the sectors or of the occupation operators is asserted.

**Slot convention.** For $\ell\ge1$, $S_\ell$ acts on $\{0,\dots,\ell-1\}$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. On one-based tuple positions use $\widehat{\pi}(k):=1+\pi(k-1)$ for $1\le k\le\ell$. Conjugation by $k\mapsto k-1$ gives $\widehat{\pi\sigma}=\widehat{\pi}\circ\widehat{\sigma}$ and $\widehat{\pi^{-1}}=\widehat{\pi}^{-1}$; thus the supplier's tensor action becomes $U_\pi(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_\ell)=v_{\widehat{\pi}^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\widehat{\pi}^{-1}(\ell)}$. The parameters of $U_\pi$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)$ remain canonical zero-based permutations.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space of finite dimension $d\ge1$ with orthonormal basis
$(e_1,\dots,e_d)$ ([[def-hilbert-space]],
[[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]). Let
$n\ge1$, and let $H^{\otimes n}$ be the $n$-fold completed tensor power with
$H^{\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$, $H^{\otimes1}:=H$ and
$H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$
([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]), and let
$P_\pm^{(n)}\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$, $n\ge1$, be the permutation
projections of [[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. For a
multi-index $i=(i_1,\dots,i_n)\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n$ write
$$e_i:=e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_n},\qquad |i|_j:=\#\{k:i_k=j\}\ (j=1,\dots,d).$$
For $J\subseteq\{1,\dots,d\}$ with $|J|=n$, written $J=\{j_1<\cdots<j_n\}$, put
$$e_J^\wedge:=\frac1{\sqrt{n!}}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\, e_{j_{\widehat{\sigma}(1)}}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_{\widehat{\sigma}(n)}},$$
and for $\lambda\in W(n,d):=\{\lambda\in\mathbb N^d:\sum_j\lambda_j=n\}$ put
$\operatorname{orb}(\lambda):=\{c\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n:|c|=\lambda\}$ and
$m_\lambda:=\sum_{c\in\operatorname{orb}(\lambda)}e_c$. Then:

(a) *product basis*: $(e_i)_{i\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n}$ is an orthonormal basis of
$H^{\otimes n}$, and $\dim H^{\otimes n}=d^n$;

(b) *Slater basis*: for every $J$ with $|J|=n$ one has
$e_J^\wedge=\sqrt{n!}\,P_-^{(n)}(e_{j_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_n})$ and the
family $(e_J^\wedge)_{J\subseteq\{1,\dots,d\},\ |J|=n}$ is an orthonormal family whose
closed linear span is $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}$; it is therefore an
orthonormal basis of $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}$,
$\dim\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}=\binom dn$, and
$\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}=\{0\}$ when $n>d$. Moreover for every multi-index
$i$ one has $P_-^{(n)}(e_i)=0$ when two entries of $i$ coincide, and
$$P_-^{(n)}(e_i)=\operatorname{sgn}(\rho_i)\,\frac{e_J^\wedge}{\sqrt{n!}}$$
when the entries of $i$ are pairwise distinct with underlying set $J$ and
$\rho_i\in S_n$ is the unique permutation with $i_k=j_{\widehat{\rho_i}(k)}$;

(c) *symmetric basis*: for every $\lambda\in W(n,d)$ the vector $m_\lambda$ is
nonzero, the family $(m_\lambda)_{\lambda\in W(n,d)}$ is orthogonal,
$U_\pi m_\lambda=m_\lambda$ for every $\pi\in S_n$, and for every multi-index
$i$ there is a real number $\gamma_i>0$ with
$P_+^{(n)}(e_i)=\gamma_i\,m_{|i|}$; consequently
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ is the linear span of $(m_\lambda)$, the family
$(m_\lambda)$ is an orthogonal basis of $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$, and
$\dim\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}=\binom{n+d-1}{n}$;

(d) *occupation operators*: for $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ the map
$$N_j:H^{\otimes n}\to H^{\otimes n},\qquad N_jx:=\sum_{i\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n}|i|_j\,\langle x,e_i\rangle\,e_i,$$
is a self-adjoint bounded endomorphism, the $N_j$ commute pairwise,
$\sum_{j=1}^dN_j=nI$, and
$$N_je_J^\wedge=\mathbf 1_J(j)\,e_J^\wedge,\qquad N_jm_\lambda=\lambda_j\,m_\lambda .$$
Consequently both sectors are invariant under every $N_j$, the joint
eigenspaces of $(N_1,\dots,N_d)$ inside $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}$ are the
lines $\mathbb Ce_J^\wedge$ (one for each $n$-element subset $J$, with
eigenvalue vector $\mathbf 1_J$), and the joint eigenspaces inside
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ are the lines $\mathbb Cm_\lambda$ (one for each
$\lambda\in W(n,d)$, with eigenvalue vector $\lambda$).

For a finite set $A$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$ put

$$[A]^{k} := \{\, S \subseteq A \ :\ \lvert S\rvert = k \,\},$$

the set of $k$-element subsets of $A$. Every $S \subseteq A$ is finite
([[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]]), so the condition $\lvert S\rvert = k$ makes
sense for every subset.

**$[A]^{k}$ is finite.** It is a subset of $\mathcal{P}(A)$, which is finite by
[[cor-cardinality-of-the-power-set]], so [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]] applies.

**$\lvert [A]^{k}\rvert$ depends only on $\lvert A\rvert$.** Let $h : A \to A'$ be
a bijection of finite sets. The direct image map $S \mapsto h[S]$ carries
$[A]^{k}$ into $[A']^{k}$, because $h$ restricted to $S$ is a bijection of $S$
onto $h[S]$ and so $\lvert h[S]\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = k$ by the transport
clause of [[def-finite-cardinality]]; the map $T \mapsto h^{-1}[T]$ is its
two-sided inverse, since $h^{-1}[h[S]] = S$ and $h[h^{-1}[T]] = T$ for a
bijection $h$. So $[A]^{k} \approx [A']^{k}$ and the two have the same
cardinality.

**Definition.** For $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$ set

$$\binom{n}{k} := \big\lvert\, [n]^{k} \,\big\rvert \in \mathbb{N},$$

the **binomial coefficient**. By the previous paragraph and $\lvert n\rvert = n$,

$$\big\lvert [A]^{k}\big\rvert = \binom{\lvert A\rvert}{k} \qquad \text{for every finite } A .$$

**$\binom{n}{k}$ is a count, so it is a natural number by construction.** It is
*not* defined as $n!/(k!\,(n-k)!)$: that expression involves a division, hence
lives in $\mathbb{R}$, and the assertion that its value is a natural number is a
theorem, proved in [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]]. Defining the coefficient as a
count makes integrality free and leaves the closed formula something to prove.

**Boundary values, read off the definition and not stipulated.**

- $\binom{n}{0} = 1$ **for every $n$, including $n = 0$**: the subsets of $n$ of
  cardinality $0$ are exactly the subsets equal to $\varnothing$
  ([[def-finite-cardinality]], clause (b)), so $[n]^{0} = \{\varnothing\}$, a
  one-element set. No empty-product convention is involved.
- $\binom{n}{n} = 1$: if $S \subseteq n$ has $\lvert S\rvert = n = \lvert n\rvert$
  then $S = n$ by clause 3 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $[n]^{n} = \{n\}$.
- $\binom{n}{k} = 0$ for $k > n$: a subset $S \subseteq n$ has
  $\lvert S\rvert \le n$ by clause 2 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $\lvert S\rvert = k > n$ is impossible and $[n]^{k} = \varnothing$
  ([[lem-nat-trichotomy]]).
- $\binom{n}{1} = n$: a subset of cardinality $1$ is $\{x\}$ for exactly one
  $x \in n$, since $\lvert S\rvert = 1$ means $S \approx \{0\}$; so
  $S \mapsto$ its unique element is a bijection $[n]^{1} \to n$.
- $\binom{0}{0} = 1$ and $\binom{0}{k} = 0$ for $k \ge 1$, both instances of the
  above.

Let $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$ with $k \le n$. Then, in $\mathbb{N}$,

$$\binom{n}{k}\cdot k!\cdot (n-k)! = n! ,$$

and consequently:

1. $\binom{n}{k}\cdot k! = n^{\underline{k}}$
   ([[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]);
2. **integrality**: in $\mathbb{R}$,
   $\iota\binom{n}{k} = \dfrac{\iota(n!)}{\iota(k!)\,\iota((n-k)!)}$, so the
   familiar quotient $n!/(k!\,(n-k)!)$ is the canonical natural of a natural
   number, namely of the count $\binom{n}{k}$;
3. **symmetry**: $\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n}{n-k}$.

Here $\iota$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]] and $n-k$ the
truncated difference, which for $k \le n$ is the ordinary one.

Let $m \ge 1$ and write $m = \sigma(M)$, so $M = m-1$. Then for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$

$$\big\lvert\mathcal{W}(n,m)\big\rvert = \binom{n+m-1}{\,m-1\,} = \binom{n+M}{M},$$

and the map
$k \mapsto \big\{\, \big(\sum_{j<\sigma(i)} k_j\big) + i \ :\ i < M \,\big\}$
is a bijection of $\mathcal{W}(n,m)$ onto the set of $M$-element subsets of
$n+M$.

Moreover, for $m \ge 1$ **and $n \ge 1$**,

$$\big\lvert\mathcal{C}(n,m)\big\rvert = \binom{n-1}{\,m-1\,}.$$

**The hypothesis $m \ge 1$ is not decoration.** At $m = 0$ the expression
$\binom{n+m-1}{m-1}$ would require the value $m-1$ at $m = 0$, and
[[def-composition-of-a-natural-number]] records the true counts there:
$\lvert\mathcal{W}(0,0)\rvert = 1$ and $\lvert\mathcal{W}(n,0)\rvert = 0$ for
$n \ge 1$. The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ in the second display is equally load
bearing: at $n = 0$, $m = 1$ the formula would give $\binom{0}{0} = 1$ while
$\mathcal{C}(0,1) = \varnothing$.

1. **The row sum.** For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, in $\mathbb{N}$,
   $$\sum_{k<n+1}\binom{n}{k} = 2^{\,n} .$$
2. **The alternating row sum.** For every $n \ge 1$, in $\mathbb{R}$,
   $$\sum_{k<n+1}(-1)^{k}\,\iota\binom{n}{k} = 0 .$$

**Clause 2 is false at $n = 0$**, where the sum has the single term
$(-1)^{0}\iota\binom{0}{0} = 1$. The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is therefore part of the
statement, and this page's companion records the version that drops it as a false
statement.

derivations.claim: [Fermionic configurations] Let $J\subseteq\{1,\dots,d\}$ have $|J|=n$; its indicator $\mathbf 1_J$ lies in $\{0,1\}^d$ with $\sum_j\mathbf 1_J(j)=n$. Conversely, if $\lambda\in\{0,1\}^d$ has $\sum_j\lambda_j=n$, then $J_\lambda:=\{j:\lambda_j=1\}$ satisfies $|J_\lambda|=n$ and $\mathbf 1_{J_\lambda}=\lambda$. The two assignments are inverse bijections, so the number of fermionic configurations of total occupation $n$ equals the number of $n$-element subsets, which is $\binom dn$ by [F2]. For $n\ge1$, this is $\dim\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}$ by [F1]; for $n=0$, the dimension is $1=\binom d0$ by [F0] and the boundary value in [F2]. This proves (a)'s dimension assertion in all cases.

[Bosonic configurations] If $n=0$, then $W(0,d)=\{\mathbf 0\}$ and $m_{\mathbf 0}=1$ by [F0], so its assignment is a bijection onto the single basis line of $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. If $n\ge1$, the assignment $\lambda\mapsto m_\lambda$ is injective by the linear independence of the orthogonal family [F1], and its image spans $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$, so it is a bijection onto the set of basis lines. In either case, the number of its elements is $|W(n,d)|=\binom{n+d-1}{d-1}=\binom{n+d-1}{n}$ by [F3] and [F2], the first assertion of (b).

[Truncated bosonic dimension] For $n\ge1$ the dimension $\dim\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}=\binom{n+d-1}{n}=\binom{n+d-1}{d-1}$ is given by [F1] and [F2]; at $n=0$ it is $1=\binom{d-1}{d-1}$ by [F0] and the boundary value of the binomial coefficient. Thus $\sum_{n=0}^{N}\dim\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}=\sum_{n=0}^{N}\binom{n+d-1}{d-1}$. Substituting $i:=n+d-1$, the terms with $i<d-1$ vanish by the boundary values of the binomial coefficient, so the hockey stick [F4] with $k=d-1$ and upper index $N+d-1$ gives $\sum_{i=0}^{N+d-1}\binom{i}{d-1}=\binom{N+d}{d}$; this completes (b).

[Fermionic row sum] Summing the dimensions over all particle numbers, using [F0] at $n=0$ and [F1] for $1\le n\le d$ and the vanishing for $n>d$, gives $\sum_{n=0}^d\dim\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}=\sum_{n=0}^d\binom dn=2^d$ by the row sum [F5], which completes (a).

[Exclusion counts] By construction every fermionic configuration lies in $\{0,1\}^d$, so no entry is $\ge2$; for $n>d$ the set $\{0,1\}^d\cap\{\sum_j\lambda_j=n\}$ is empty because at most $d$ entries can be equal to $1$, and then $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}=\{0\}$ by [F1], while for the bosonic sector the configuration $\lambda^{(j)}$ with $\lambda^{(j)}_j=n$ and all other entries $0$ lies in $W(n,d)$ for every $j$, so no occupation bound holds there; this is (c).

[Consistency and assembly] Each $\lambda\in W(n,d)$ satisfies $\sum_j\lambda_j=n$ by definition, and each fermionic configuration in $\{0,1\}^d\cap\{\sum_j\lambda_j=n\}$ does so as well, which is (d); step 1.1 and 2.1 prove (a), steps 1.2 and 1.3 prove (b), and step 2.2 proves (c). Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ be a finite list of $R$-modules. Any parenthesized tensor product

$$T=M_1\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RM_k$$

represents $R$-multilinear maps from $M_1\times\cdots\times M_k$: for every $R$-module $P$, composition with $(m_1,\ldots,m_k)\mapsto m_1\otimes\cdots\otimes m_k$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{Hom}_R(T,P)$ to the set of multilinear maps into $P$. Different parenthesizations are connected by the unique isomorphism preserving pure tensors.

For $k=0$, take $T=R$ and identify zero-variable multilinear maps with chosen elements of $P$. For $k=1$, take $T=M_1$.

Let $V$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and let
$W\subseteq V$ be a normed subspace. If $W$ admits an ordered basis of finite
length, including length zero, then $W$ is closed in $V$. This holds in ZF,
without a choice axiom; the ambient space need not be complete.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first argument
([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), let
$H\widehat\otimes H$ be its completed tensor square with inclusion $\kappa$
([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]), and for $n=2$ let
$(U_\pi)_{\pi\in S_2}$ and the projections $P_\pm^{(2)}$ be those of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Write
$\tau:=U_{(0\,1)}$ for the **exchange operator**, so that
$\tau\bigl(\kappa(u\otimes v)\bigr)=\kappa(v\otimes u)$ for $u,v\in H$; in the
sequel the inclusion is suppressed and $u\otimes v$ denotes
$\kappa(u\otimes v)$. Then:

(a) $\tau$ is self-adjoint and $\tau^2=I$; consequently $\tau$ is an isometry
with $\tau^{-1}=\tau=\tau^{*}$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]);

(b) $P_+^{(2)}=\tfrac12(I+\tau)$ and $P_-^{(2)}=\tfrac12(I-\tau)$, and
$$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(2)}=\{x\in H\widehat\otimes H:\tau x=x\},\qquad \operatorname{ran}P_-^{(2)}=\{x\in H\widehat\otimes H:\tau x=-x\};$$

(c) for all $u,v\in H$,
$$\|u\otimes v+v\otimes u\|^{2}=2\bigl(\|u\|^{2}\|v\|^{2}+|\langle u,v\rangle|^{2}\bigr), \qquad \|u\otimes v-v\otimes u\|^{2}=2\bigl(\|u\|^{2}\|v\|^{2}-|\langle u,v\rangle|^{2}\bigr);$$
in particular, if $u,v$ are orthonormal, then
$s:=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(u\otimes v+v\otimes u)$ and
$a:=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(u\otimes v-v\otimes u)$ are orthonormal, $\tau s=s$ and
$\tau a=-a$, and both $\operatorname{ran}P_\pm^{(2)}$ are nonzero;

(d) whenever $u,v\in H$ are orthonormal,
$\tau\kappa(u\otimes v)\ne\kappa(u\otimes v)$. Consequently, if $H$
contains an orthonormal pair (equivalently, $\dim H\ge2$), both exchange
eigenspaces contain nonzero vectors and $\tau\ne I$. If $H=\{0\}$ or
$\dim H=1$, then $\tau=I$, $P_+^{(2)}=I$ and $P_-^{(2)}=0$; for $H=\{0\}$
the tensor square and both ranges are zero.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}\in H$ write $v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1}\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor.

(a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with

$$U_\pi(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=v_{\pi^{-1}(0)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n-1)},$$

and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$.

(b) The operators

$$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$

(with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections.

(c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$.

(d) If $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}$ have a repeated factor, that is, $v_i=v_j$ for some distinct $i,j\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, then $P_-(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=0$.

Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,H',K,K'$ be complex Hilbert spaces and let $S\in\mathcal B(H,H')$, $T\in\mathcal B(K,K')$ be bounded linear operators ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Write $H\widehat\otimes K$ for the completion of the algebraic tensor product constructed in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], with inclusion $\kappa$.

(a) There is a unique bounded linear operator $S\otimes T: H\widehat\otimes K\to H'\widehat\otimes K'$ with $(S\otimes T)\kappa(u\otimes v)=\kappa'(Su\otimes Tv)$ for all $u\in H$, $v\in K$, and it satisfies $\|S\otimes T\|\le\|S\|\,\|T\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]).

(b) For Hilbert spaces $H'',K''$ and bounded $S':H''\to H$, $T':K''\to K$, one has $(S\otimes T)(S'\otimes T')=(SS')\otimes(TT')$. In particular, for endomorphisms $S:H\to H$, $T:K\to K$, the endomorphisms $S\otimes I_K$ and $I_H\otimes T$ commute and their composite is $S\otimes T$.

(c) The Hilbert adjoint ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]) is $(S\otimes T)^*=S^*\otimes T^*$.

(d) If $S,T$ are unitary, then so is $S\otimes T$. No extension of unbounded maps, and no algebraic manipulation of domains of unbounded operators, is asserted.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $m,n\in\mathbb N$. The standard finite free modules satisfy

$$R^m\otimes_RR^n\cong R^{mn},$$

with the tensor products of standard basis vectors corresponding to the standard basis indexed by $m\times n$.

If $F$ is a field and $V,W$ are finite-dimensional $F$-vector spaces, then

$$\dim_F(V\otimes_FW)=(\dim_FV)(\dim_FW).$$

Both assertions include a zero rank or zero-dimensional factor.

**Slot convention.** For $\ell\ge1$, $S_\ell$ acts on $\{0,\dots,\ell-1\}$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. On one-based tuple positions use $\widehat{\pi}(k):=1+\pi(k-1)$ for $1\le k\le\ell$. Conjugation by $k\mapsto k-1$ gives $\widehat{\pi\sigma}=\widehat{\pi}\circ\widehat{\sigma}$ and $\widehat{\pi^{-1}}=\widehat{\pi}^{-1}$; thus the supplier's tensor action becomes $U_\pi(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_\ell)=v_{\widehat{\pi}^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\widehat{\pi}^{-1}(\ell)}$. The parameters of $U_\pi$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)$ remain canonical zero-based permutations.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space of finite dimension $d\ge1$ with orthonormal basis
$(e_1,\dots,e_d)$ ([[def-hilbert-space]],
[[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]). Let
$n\ge1$, and let $H^{\otimes n}$ be the $n$-fold completed tensor power with
$H^{\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$, $H^{\otimes1}:=H$ and
$H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$
([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]), and let
$P_\pm^{(n)}\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$, $n\ge1$, be the permutation
projections of [[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. For a
multi-index $i=(i_1,\dots,i_n)\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n$ write
$$e_i:=e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_n},\qquad |i|_j:=\#\{k:i_k=j\}\ (j=1,\dots,d).$$
For $J\subseteq\{1,\dots,d\}$ with $|J|=n$, written $J=\{j_1<\cdots<j_n\}$, put
$$e_J^\wedge:=\frac1{\sqrt{n!}}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\, e_{j_{\widehat{\sigma}(1)}}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_{\widehat{\sigma}(n)}},$$
and for $\lambda\in W(n,d):=\{\lambda\in\mathbb N^d:\sum_j\lambda_j=n\}$ put
$\operatorname{orb}(\lambda):=\{c\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n:|c|=\lambda\}$ and
$m_\lambda:=\sum_{c\in\operatorname{orb}(\lambda)}e_c$. Then:

(a) *product basis*: $(e_i)_{i\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n}$ is an orthonormal basis of
$H^{\otimes n}$, and $\dim H^{\otimes n}=d^n$;

(b) *Slater basis*: for every $J$ with $|J|=n$ one has
$e_J^\wedge=\sqrt{n!}\,P_-^{(n)}(e_{j_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_n})$ and the
family $(e_J^\wedge)_{J\subseteq\{1,\dots,d\},\ |J|=n}$ is an orthonormal family whose
closed linear span is $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}$; it is therefore an
orthonormal basis of $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}$,
$\dim\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}=\binom dn$, and
$\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}=\{0\}$ when $n>d$. Moreover for every multi-index
$i$ one has $P_-^{(n)}(e_i)=0$ when two entries of $i$ coincide, and
$$P_-^{(n)}(e_i)=\operatorname{sgn}(\rho_i)\,\frac{e_J^\wedge}{\sqrt{n!}}$$
when the entries of $i$ are pairwise distinct with underlying set $J$ and
$\rho_i\in S_n$ is the unique permutation with $i_k=j_{\widehat{\rho_i}(k)}$;

(c) *symmetric basis*: for every $\lambda\in W(n,d)$ the vector $m_\lambda$ is
nonzero, the family $(m_\lambda)_{\lambda\in W(n,d)}$ is orthogonal,
$U_\pi m_\lambda=m_\lambda$ for every $\pi\in S_n$, and for every multi-index
$i$ there is a real number $\gamma_i>0$ with
$P_+^{(n)}(e_i)=\gamma_i\,m_{|i|}$; consequently
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ is the linear span of $(m_\lambda)$, the family
$(m_\lambda)$ is an orthogonal basis of $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$, and
$\dim\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}=\binom{n+d-1}{n}$;

(d) *occupation operators*: for $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ the map
$$N_j:H^{\otimes n}\to H^{\otimes n},\qquad N_jx:=\sum_{i\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n}|i|_j\,\langle x,e_i\rangle\,e_i,$$
is a self-adjoint bounded endomorphism, the $N_j$ commute pairwise,
$\sum_{j=1}^dN_j=nI$, and
$$N_je_J^\wedge=\mathbf 1_J(j)\,e_J^\wedge,\qquad N_jm_\lambda=\lambda_j\,m_\lambda .$$
Consequently both sectors are invariant under every $N_j$, the joint
eigenspaces of $(N_1,\dots,N_d)$ inside $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}$ are the
lines $\mathbb Ce_J^\wedge$ (one for each $n$-element subset $J$, with
eigenvalue vector $\mathbf 1_J$), and the joint eigenspaces inside
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ are the lines $\mathbb Cm_\lambda$ (one for each
$\lambda\in W(n,d)$, with eigenvalue vector $\lambda$).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). By the orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]) every $x\in H$ has a unique representation

$$x=P_Mx+(x-P_Mx),\qquad P_Mx\in M,\quad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp ,$$

and the **Hilbert orthogonal projection onto $M$** is the map

$$P_M:H\longrightarrow M\subseteq H,\qquad x\longmapsto P_Mx ,$$

assigning to $x$ its unique $M$-component. Its defining properties are therefore

$$P_Mx\in M,\qquad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp\qquad(x\in H),$$

which characterise $P_M$ uniquely: a map with these defining properties must agree with the $M$-component of the unique decomposition of each $x$.

**Agreement with the finite-dimensional projection.** If $V$ is a finite-dimensional inner-product space and $W\subseteq V$ a subspace, then [[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]] writes $V=W\oplus W^\perp$ and [[def-orthogonal-projection]] defines $P_Wv$ as the unique $W$-component of $v$; the defining properties displayed above are the same, so they define the same map on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.

**Range and kernel.** $P_Mx\in M$ for every $x$, and $P_Mm=m$ for $m\in M$ because $m=m+0$ with $0\in M^\perp$; conversely $P_Mx=0$ says exactly that $x=x-0\in M^\perp$. Hence the range of $P_M$ is $M$ and its kernel is $M^\perp$, and $P_M$ is the identity on $M$ and zero on $M^\perp$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}\in H$ write $v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1}\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor.

(a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with

$$U_\pi(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=v_{\pi^{-1}(0)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n-1)},$$

and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$.

(b) The operators

$$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$

(with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections.

(c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$.

(d) If $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}$ have a repeated factor, that is, $v_i=v_j$ for some distinct $i,j\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, then $P_-(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=0$.

derivations.claim: [Identification] By [F1] the inclusion $\kappa:H\odot V\to H\widehat\otimes V$ is a linear isometry with dense image; if $(e_1,\dots,e_m)$ and $(f_1,\dots,f_k)$ are orthonormal bases of $H$ and $V$, then the $mk$ elements $e_a\otimes f_b$ span the algebraic tensor product by bilinearity, so $\kappa[H\odot V]$ is a finite-dimensional subspace of the Hilbert space $H\widehat\otimes V$, hence closed by [F3], and a dense closed subspace is the whole space; thus $\kappa$ is onto and identifies the two spaces, and the same argument applies to the algebraic and completed tensor products of $H\otimes V$ with itself and of $H\otimes H$ with $V\otimes V$, whose algebraic parts are spanned by finitely many elementary tensors. This proves (a).

[The regrouping map and its inverse] Define $\Phi(u,v,\chi,\chi'):=(u\otimes v)\otimes(\chi\otimes\chi')$ for $u,v\in H$, $\chi,\chi'\in V$; it is multilinear in its four arguments, so by [F2] it corresponds to a unique linear map on the four-fold algebraic tensor product and, by the parenthesization independence of [F2] together with the identification of step 1.1, to a unique linear map $\Theta$ on $(H\otimes V)\widehat\otimes(H\otimes V)$ with the displayed values on elementary tensors; uniqueness holds because those elementary tensors span the space. Likewise $\Psi\bigl((u\otimes v)\otimes(\chi\otimes\chi')\bigr):=(u\otimes\chi)\otimes(v\otimes\chi')$ is multilinear and defines a linear map $\Psi$ on $(H\otimes H)\widehat\otimes(V\otimes V)$. On elementary tensors $\Psi\Theta=\mathrm{id}$ and $\Theta\Psi=\mathrm{id}$, and two linear maps agreeing on a spanning set agree everywhere; hence $\Theta$ is a linear isomorphism with inverse $\Psi$, which is the existence and inverse statement of (b).

[Unitarity] For elementary tensors $x=(u\otimes\chi)\otimes(v\otimes\chi')$ and $y=(u'\otimes\chi'')\otimes(v'\otimes\chi''')$ in the domain the inner-product identities of [F1] give $\langle\Theta x,\Theta y\rangle=\langle u\otimes v,u'\otimes v'\rangle\langle\chi\otimes\chi',\chi''\otimes\chi'''\rangle=\langle u,u'\rangle\langle v,v'\rangle\langle\chi,\chi''\rangle\langle\chi',\chi'''\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle$; the difference of the two sesquilinear forms vanishes on all pairs of elementary tensors, and since every vector is a finite sum of elementary tensors by [F1] it vanishes identically, so $\Theta$ is an isometry; being invertible by step 2.1 it is unitary, which completes (b).

[Intertwining with the exchange operators] For $u,v\in H$, $\chi,\chi'\in V$ one computes with [F4] and [F5] that $\Theta\tau_{H\otimes V}\bigl((u\otimes\chi)\otimes(v\otimes\chi')\bigr)=\Theta\bigl((v\otimes\chi')\otimes(u\otimes\chi)\bigr)=(v\otimes u)\otimes(\chi'\otimes\chi)$ and $(\tau_H\otimes\tau_V)\Theta\bigl((u\otimes\chi)\otimes(v\otimes\chi')\bigr)=(\tau_H\otimes\tau_V)\bigl((u\otimes v)\otimes(\chi\otimes\chi')\bigr)=(v\otimes u)\otimes(\chi'\otimes\chi)$; both sides are bounded linear maps agreeing on the spanning set of elementary tensors, so they agree everywhere, which is (c).

[Symmetriser identities] By [F4], $P_\pm^{(H\otimes V)}=\frac12(I\pm\tau_{H\otimes V})$, $P_\pm^{(H)}=\frac12(I\pm\tau_H)$ and $P_\pm^{(V)}=\frac12(I\pm\tau_V)$; using step 3.2 to move $\Theta$ past $\tau_{H\otimes V}$ and the linearity and multiplicativity of the tensor product of operators [F5], one obtains on the whole space $\Theta P_-^{(H\otimes V)}=\frac12\Theta-\frac12(\tau_H\otimes\tau_V)\Theta=\bigl(\frac12-\frac12\tau_H\otimes\tau_V\bigr)\Theta=\bigl(P_-^{(H)}\otimes P_+^{(V)}+P_+^{(H)}\otimes P_-^{(V)}\bigr)\Theta$, because $\frac12(I-\tau_H\otimes\tau_V)=\frac12(I-\tau_H)\otimes\frac12(I+\tau_V)+\frac12(I+\tau_H)\otimes\frac12(I-\tau_V)$ and its sign-reversed analogue are identities of bounded operators; this proves the first assertion of (d), and the computation with both signs reversed gives the second.

[Direct-sum decompositions] By [F7] the operators $P_-^{(H)}\otimes P_+^{(V)}$ and $P_+^{(H)}\otimes P_-^{(V)}$ are orthogonal projections whose product is $(P_-^{(H)}P_+^{(H)})\otimes(P_+^{(V)}P_-^{(V)})=0$, so their sum is an orthogonal projection with range the orthogonal direct sum of the two ranges; by step 4.1 and the unitarity of step 3.1, the image of $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(H\otimes V)}$ under $\Theta$ is that direct sum, and the same argument with the second identity of step 4.1 gives the symmetric-sector decomposition, completing (d).

[Vector identities] Applying the first identity of step 4.1 to the elementary tensor $(u\otimes\chi)\otimes(v\otimes\chi')$ and using the linearity of $\Theta$ and of tensor products of operators gives $\Theta P_-^{(H\otimes V)}\bigl((u\otimes\chi)\otimes(v\otimes\chi')\bigr)=\bigl(P_-^{(H)}\otimes P_+^{(V)}+P_+^{(H)}\otimes P_-^{(V)}\bigr)\bigl((u\otimes v)\otimes(\chi\otimes\chi')\bigr)=P_+^{(H)}(u\otimes v)\otimes P_-^{(V)}(\chi\otimes\chi')+P_-^{(H)}(u\otimes v)\otimes P_+^{(V)}(\chi\otimes\chi')$, which is the first identity of (e); the second follows in the same way from the second identity of step 4.1.

[Dimensions] By step 5.1 and the unitarity of step 3.1, $\dim\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(H\otimes V)}=\dim(\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(H)}\otimes\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(V)})+\dim(\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(H)}\otimes\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(V)})$; by [F6] applied to the $m$- and $k$-dimensional spaces this is $\binom m2\binom{k+1}2+\binom{m+1}2\binom k2$, which are the displayed summand dimensions, and expanding the two products gives $\frac{m(m-1)k(k+1)+m(m+1)k(k-1)}4=\frac{mk(mk-1)}2=\binom{mk}2$, which is (f).

[Assembly] Step 1.1 proves (a), steps 2.1 and 3.1 prove (b), step 3.2 proves (c), steps 4.1 and 5.1 prove (d), step 5.2 proves (e) and step 6.1 proves (f).
